guided.title: Label the first products
guided.prompt: For products with `product_id` up to 12, return `product_id`, `product_name` and `price_label` (in that order). The label is `cheap` when `unit_price` is below 15, `mid` when it is from 15 up to but not including 40, and `dear` otherwise. Order by `product_id`.
guided.starter:
-- Label products with product_id <= 12 as cheap, mid or dear
SELECT product_id, product_name, 'mid' AS price_label
FROM products
WHERE product_id <= 12
ORDER BY product_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT product_id, product_name,
       CASE
         WHEN unit_price < 15 THEN 'cheap'
         WHEN unit_price < 40 THEN 'mid'
         ELSE 'dear'
       END AS price_label
FROM products
WHERE product_id <= 12
ORDER BY product_id;
hints: The starter gives every row the same label. A CASE expression chooses the label per row.
Test the lowest band first: WHEN unit_price < 15 THEN 'cheap'. The next WHEN only sees prices of 15 or more.
CASE WHEN unit_price < 15 THEN 'cheap' WHEN unit_price < 40 THEN 'mid' ELSE 'dear' END AS price_label

guided.title: Split German contact names
guided.prompt: For customers in Germany, return `customer_id`, `first_name` and `last_name` (in that order), where the contact name is split at the space with `SPLIT_PART`. Order by `customer_id`.
guided.starter:
-- First and last name of German contacts
SELECT customer_id, contact_name AS first_name, contact_name AS last_name
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'Germany'
ORDER BY customer_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       SPLIT_PART(contact_name, ' ', 1) AS first_name,
       SPLIT_PART(contact_name, ' ', 2) AS last_name
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'Germany'
ORDER BY customer_id;
hints: The starter repeats the full contact name. You need a function that returns one piece of the text.
SPLIT_PART(text, delimiter, n) returns the n-th piece, counting from 1. The delimiter here is a space.
SPLIT_PART(contact_name, ' ', 1) AS first_name and SPLIT_PART(contact_name, ' ', 2) AS last_name

guided.title: Gross prices of expensive products
guided.prompt: For products with `unit_price` of 50 or more, return `product_id`, `name_upper` (the product name in upper case) and `gross_price` (the price times 1.2, rounded to 2 decimals), in that order. Order by `product_id`.
guided.starter:
-- Upper-case names and gross prices (price * 1.2) for products priced 50 or more
SELECT product_id, product_name AS name_upper, unit_price AS gross_price
FROM products
WHERE unit_price >= 50
ORDER BY product_id;
guided.solution:
SELECT product_id,
       UPPER(product_name) AS name_upper,
       ROUND(unit_price * 1.2, 2) AS gross_price
FROM products
WHERE unit_price >= 50
ORDER BY product_id;
hints: The WHERE and ORDER BY are right. Two select-list expressions are wrong.
UPPER(text) changes case; ROUND(number, 2) rounds to two decimals.
UPPER(product_name) AS name_upper, ROUND(unit_price * 1.2, 2) AS gross_price

guided.title: Shipped and open orders per carrier
guided.prompt: For each carrier (`ship_via`) return `orders` (all orders), `shipped` (orders whose `shipped_date` is not NULL) and `open_orders` (orders whose `shipped_date` is NULL), in that order after `ship_via`. Use conditional aggregation, with no `WHERE`. Order by `ship_via`.
guided.starter:
-- Orders, shipped and open per carrier
SELECT ship_via, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(*) AS shipped, COUNT(*) AS open_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY ship_via
ORDER BY ship_via;
guided.solution:
SELECT ship_via,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN shipped_date IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
       SUM(CASE WHEN shipped_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS open_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY ship_via
ORDER BY ship_via;
hints: All three columns of the starter count every row. Two of them must count only a subset.
Put CASE inside SUM: add 1 when the condition is true and 0 otherwise. A NULL test uses IS NULL.
SUM(CASE WHEN shipped_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS open_orders

independent.title: Price bands of active products
independent.prompt: Ignore discontinued products. Put each remaining product into a band: `low` below 20, `middle` from 20 up to but not including 50, `high` for 50 or more. Return `band`, `products` (count) and `avg_price` (average `unit_price` rounded to 2 decimals), ordered from the lowest band to the highest (lowest average first).
independent.starter:
-- Bands of active products
SELECT 'all' AS band, COUNT(*) AS products, ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE NOT discontinued;
independent.solution:
SELECT CASE
         WHEN unit_price < 20 THEN 'low'
         WHEN unit_price < 50 THEN 'middle'
         ELSE 'high'
       END AS band,
       COUNT(*) AS products,
       ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE NOT discontinued
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY avg_price;

independent.title: Late and on-time shipments by country
independent.prompt: For each `ship_country` return `orders`, `late` (orders with `shipped_date` after `required_date`), `on_time` (orders shipped on or before `required_date`) and `open_orders` (no ship date), then `pct_late`: late orders as a percentage of all orders, rounded to 1 decimal (use `100.0 *` so the division is not an integer division). Keep only countries with at least 8 orders. Order by `orders` descending, then `ship_country`.
independent.starter:
-- Late, on-time and open orders per country (countries with 8+ orders)
SELECT ship_country, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY ship_country
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 8
ORDER BY orders DESC, ship_country;
independent.solution:
SELECT ship_country,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE shipped_date > required_date) AS late,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE shipped_date <= required_date) AS on_time,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE shipped_date IS NULL) AS open_orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE shipped_date > required_date) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_late
FROM orders
GROUP BY ship_country
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 8
ORDER BY orders DESC, ship_country;

independent.title: Short names and long company names
independent.prompt: Stretch task. For customers in Germany, the UK or the USA return `customer_id`, `short_name` (the first letter of the contact's first name, then a full stop and a space, then the last name, for example `M. Anders`; build it from `SPLIT_PART`, `LEFT` and `||`) and `name_size` (`long` when `company_name` has 25 or more characters, otherwise `short`). Order by `customer_id`.
independent.starter:
-- Short contact name and company-name size for German, UK and US customers
SELECT customer_id, contact_name AS short_name, 'short' AS name_size
FROM customers
WHERE country IN ('Germany', 'UK', 'USA')
ORDER BY customer_id;
independent.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       LEFT(SPLIT_PART(contact_name, ' ', 1), 1) || '. ' || SPLIT_PART(contact_name, ' ', 2) AS short_name,
       CASE WHEN LENGTH(company_name) >= 25 THEN 'long' ELSE 'short' END AS name_size
FROM customers
WHERE country IN ('Germany', 'UK', 'USA')
ORDER BY customer_id;

checks.question: What does `SELECT 7 / 2` return in PostgreSQL?
options: An error, because 7 is not divisible by 2
checks.explanation: Both operands are integers, so the division is an integer division and the fraction is dropped: 3. Writing 7 / 2.0 or 7::numeric / 2 gives 3.5. It does not round to 4, and it is not an error.

checks.question: A product costs 20.00. Given `CASE WHEN unit_price < 30 THEN 'A' WHEN unit_price < 10 THEN 'B' ELSE 'C' END`, which label would a product at 5.00 get?
checks.explanation: The first true WHEN wins and the rest are never examined. 5.00 is below 30, so it gets A and the branch for B can never be reached. Put the narrowest condition first.

checks.question: What does `SELECT CASE WHEN 1 = 2 THEN 'yes' END` return?
options: An error, because ELSE is required
checks.explanation: When no WHEN is true and there is no ELSE, CASE returns NULL. ELSE is optional in SQL, which is why a forgotten ELSE shows up as NULL labels in a report.

checks.question: What do `SELECT 'ab' || NULL` and `SELECT CONCAT('ab', NULL)` return?
checks.explanation: The || operator returns NULL if either side is NULL, but CONCAT treats NULL as empty text. Neither writes the word NULL into the result.

checks.question: In `orders`, 100 orders exist and 50 have freight of at least 100. What does `SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN freight >= 100 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) FROM orders` return?
checks.explanation: Both the SUM result (50) and COUNT(*) (100) are integers, so the division is an integer division and the fraction 0.5 is cut to 0. Cast one side to numeric (or multiply by 1.0) to get 0.5.

checks.question: What does `SELECT POSITION('z' IN 'abc')` return?
checks.explanation: POSITION counts from 1 and returns 0 when the text is not found. It does not return NULL or -1 as some other languages and databases do.
